The First Classification of the Arabian Shield Rocks

Dr. Ahmad Redaa

2026-02-10

Lecture objectives

By the end of this lecture, students should be able to:

  • Explain the rationale behind the first stratigraphic classification of the Arabian Shield
  • Describe the Hijaz Tectonic Cycle and its three episodes
  • Relate rock groups to their tectonic environments
  • Understand the role of orogenic cycles and plutonism in Shield evolution

Historical context

  • First systematic classification proposed in the early 1970s
  • Developed before full application of plate-tectonic terrane concepts
  • Based on:
    • Stratigraphic relations
    • Rock chemistry
    • Metamorphic grade
    • Associated plutonism
  • Established the Arabian Shield as juvenile Neoproterozoic crust

Conceptual framework

  • Arabian Shield evolution occurred during the Upper Proterozoic
  • Time span: ~1050–550 Ma
  • Progressive evolution:
    • Tholeiitic → calc-alkaline → acidic / alkaline
  • Development linked to repeated deformation events:
    • Collectively termed the Hijaz Tectonic Cycle

The Hijaz Tectonic Cycle

  • Represents ~500 million years of crustal evolution
  • Divided into three stratigraphic–tectonic episodes
  • Each episode ends with a distinct orogenic event
  • Volcanism, sedimentation, deformation, and plutonism are closely linked

[A. M. S. Al-Shanti, “Geology of the Arabian Shield of Saudi Arabia,” Scientific Publishing Center, King Abdulaziz University, 2009, p.190.]

First Episode: juvenile island-arc stage

Tectonic setting

  • Oceanic to early island-arc environment
  • No continental crustal contribution
  • Dominantly tholeiitic magmatism

Main rock groups

  • Baish Group
  • Bahah Group
  • Jeddah Group

Baish Group

  • Oldest layered rocks in the Arabian Shield
  • Lithology:
    • Basalt and andesitic basalt flows
    • Volcanic breccia, tuff
    • Greywacke, conglomerate
    • Minor chert and carbonate
  • Chemical affinity:
    • Tholeiitic
  • Interpretation:
    • Primitive oceanic island-arc crust

Bahah Group

  • Conformably overlies Baish Group
  • Dominantly sedimentary:
    • Greywacke, conglomerate
    • Chert, marble, quartzite
  • Sedimentary structures:
    • Graded bedding
    • Cross-bedding
    • Ripple marks
  • Depositional environment:
    • Shallow marine turbidite basin
  • No evidence of continental detritus

Jeddah Group

  • Volcanic and volcaniclastic rocks:
    • Basalt, andesite, dacite
    • Flow breccia, welded tuff
  • Subordinate sedimentary layers:
    • Conglomerate, chert, marble
  • More evolved composition than Baish Group
  • Represents:
    • Intermediate island-arc volcanism
  • Regional greenschist metamorphism

Aqiq Orogenic Cycle

  • Terminates the First Episode
  • Characteristics:
    • Folding and faulting (N–S trends)
    • Regional greenschist facies metamorphism
  • Associated intrusions:
    • First Diorite Series
    • Gabbro, diorite, quartz diorite
  • Isotopic signature:
    • Low initial Sr ratios (~0.7029)
    • Indicates mantle-derived magma

Second Episode: mature arc and basin development

Tectonic setting

  • Mature island arc
  • Regional unconformity above First Episode rocks
  • Increased sedimentation and volcanic diversity

Main rock groups

  • Ablah Group (lower)
  • Halaban Group (upper)

Ablah Group

  • Mixed sedimentary and volcanic succession
  • Formations:
    • Rafa’a (conglomerate, greywacke, tuff)
    • Jerub (calc-alkaline volcanics)
    • Thurat (elastic sediments + volcanics)
  • Features:
    • Rapid vertical and lateral facies changes
    • Stromatolitic limestone
  • Environment:
    • Shallow intra-arc or back-arc basins

Ranyah Orogenic Cycle

  • Affects Ablah Group
  • Deformation style:
    • N–NE trending folds and faults
  • Metamorphism:
    • Greenschist to local amphibolite facies
  • Associated intrusions:
    • Second Diorite Series
    • Gabbro, diorite, trondhjemite
  • Age:
    • ~800 Ma
  • Mantle-dominated isotopic signature

Halaban Group

  • Dominantly volcanic
  • Composition:
    • Andesite, dacite, rhyolite
    • Volcaniclastic and epiclastic sediments
  • Vertical evolution:
    • Mafic to increasingly felsic upwards
  • Depositional environment:
    • Active island-arc volcanic belts
  • Chemical affinity:
    • Calc-alkaline

Yafikh Orogenic Cycle

  • Terminates Halaban Group deposition
  • Characteristics:
    • Folding, faulting, schistosity
    • Regional greenschist metamorphism
  • Intrusive suites:
    • Granite, granodiorite, quartz monzonite
  • Isotopic signature:
    • Slightly higher Sr ratios (~0.7035)
    • Suggests lower crustal involvement

Third Episode: late orogenic sedimentation

Tectonic setting

  • Regional uplift and erosion
  • Widespread basin development
  • Transition to craton stabilization

Main rock groups

  • Murdamah Group
  • Shammar Group

Murdamah Group

  • Thick clastic sedimentary succession (~2700 m)
  • Lithology:
    • Conglomerate
    • Arkosic greywacke
    • Marble
    • Sandstone and siltstone
  • Molasse-type deposits
  • Depositional interpretation:
    • Erosion of uplifted arc crust
  • Rb–Sr age:
    • ~566 Ma

Shammar Group

  • Felsic volcanic rocks:
    • Rhyolite
    • Ignimbrite
    • Pyroclastics and epiclastics
  • Occurs mainly in NE Arabian Shield
  • Lateral facies equivalent of Murdamah Group
  • Rb–Sr age:
    • ~572 Ma
  • Indicates late-stage felsic magmatism

Bishah Orogenic Cycle

  • Final tectonic event affecting the Shield
  • Deformation:
    • Regional folding and faulting
  • Metamorphism:
    • Greenschist facies
  • Plutonism:
    • Granite, granodiorite, quartz monzonite
    • Alkaline and peralkaline granites
  • Marks final cratonization at ~550 Ma

Modern tectonic framework (context)

  • Arabian Shield forms part of the East African–Arabian Orogen
  • Built through:
    • Multiple juvenile arc terranes
    • Subduction, accretion, collision, and strike-slip translation
  • Characterized by:
    • Diachronous deformation
    • Discrete suture zones and ophiolites
    • High-precision geochronology

Limitation 1: Implicit plate-tectonic framework

First classification

  • Plate tectonics is implicit rather than explicit
  • Uses descriptive terms such as:
    • Tectonic cycles
    • Episodes
    • Orogenies
  • Does not explicitly define:
    • Plate boundaries
    • Subduction polarity
    • Relative plate motions

Modern models

  • Explicit reconstruction of:
    • Convergent margins
    • Subduction geometry and polarity
    • Arc–arc and arc–continent collisions

Key limitation: Lack of explicit kinematic plate-tectonic constraints.

Limitation 2: Absence of the terrane concept

First classification

  • Treats the Arabian Shield as:
    • A laterally continuous arc system
  • Assumes regional correlation of lithostratigraphic groups

Modern models

  • Shield is a collage of discrete terranes
  • Each terrane has:
    • Independent magmatic and tectonic histories
    • Distinct age ranges and metamorphic evolution
  • Terranes are separated by suture zones

Key limitation: Oversimplification of the Shield’s lateral crustal heterogeneity.

Limitation 3: Emphasis on vertical (time-controlled) evolution

First classification

  • Interprets magmatic evolution as:
    • Tholeiitic → calc-alkaline → felsic
  • Assumes this trend reflects temporal evolution within one arc

Modern understanding

  • Similar compositions can form:
    • Simultaneously in different arcs
    • In different tectonic settings
  • Magma chemistry reflects tectonic environment, not only age

Key limitation:
Geochemical evolution is treated as mainly time-dependent, rather than tectonically controlled.

Limitation 4: Broad regional orogenies

First classification

  • Defines large-scale, Shield-wide orogenies:
    • Aqiq
    • Ranyah
    • Yafikh
    • Bishah
  • Implies synchronous deformation over wide regions

Modern models

  • Deformation is:
    • Diachronous
    • Localized along sutures and shear zones
  • Many “orogenies” represent:
    • Multiple accretion events
    • Progressive transpressional deformation

Key limitation:
Regional orogenies obscure localized accretionary processes.

Limitation 5: Limited recognition of suture zones and ophiolites

First classification

  • Ophiolitic rocks:
    • Poorly recognized or inconsistently classified
  • Sutures are not emphasized as primary tectonic features

Modern models

  • Ophiolites mark:
    • Closed ocean basins
    • Terrane boundaries
  • Sutures are fundamental to Shield architecture

Key limitation:
Inadequate identification of ocean-closure structures.

Limitation 6: Coarse geochronological resolution

First classification

  • Relies mainly on:
    • Rb–Sr whole-rock ages
    • Broad age brackets
  • Many correlations are interpretive

Modern models

  • Use high-precision:
    • U–Pb zircon dating
    • Lu–Hf isotope systematics
  • Resolve short-lived and overlapping tectonic events

Key limitation:
Temporal resolution insufficient for terrane-scale reconstruction.

Limitation 7: Underestimation of strike-slip tectonics

First classification

  • Najd Fault System treated mainly as:
    • A late structural overprint

Modern interpretation

  • Najd Fault System is a:
    • Major transcurrent tectonic system
    • Mechanism for terrane translation and escape tectonics
    • Key control on basin development and magmatism

Key limitation:
The tectonic role of strike-slip deformation is underestimated.

Limitation 8: Limited global tectonic integration

First classification

  • Focuses on internal Shield evolution
  • Minimal linkage to:
    • Gondwana assembly
    • Pan-African orogeny
    • Global Neoproterozoic plate systems

Modern models

  • Arabian Shield is integral to:
    • East African–Arabian Orogen
    • Global Neoproterozoic accretionary systems

Key limitation:
The Shield is treated as regionally isolated, not globally connected.

Summary comparison

Aspect First Classification Modern Tectonic Models
Plate tectonics Implicit Explicit
Terranes Not defined Fundamental
Subduction polarity Undefined Defined
Orogenies Broad, regional Localized, diachronous
Sutures & ophiolites Poorly resolved Key elements
Geochronology Low resolution High precision
Strike-slip tectonics Minor role Major role
Global context Limited Fully integrated
